---
title: "Shortest Paths: Relax an Upper Bound"
description: "A mathematical interview pattern explained by a small example and proof."
---

## Recognition trigger

Weighted graph minimum-cost routes, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford reasoning.

## Main question

**Why can we update a known distance when a new path through another vertex is cheaper?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
d[v]\leftarrow\min(d[v],d[u]+w(u,v))
$$

**Every symbol explained:** d[v] is the best currently known upper bound on distance from the start to vertex v; d[u] is the known upper bound for u; w(u,v) is edge cost from u to v; min keeps the lower candidate.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Suppose a direct path from start S to B costs 9. The best route to A costs 3 and edge A→B costs 4. Relaxation sets d[B]=min(9,3+4)=7, improving the route.

## Derivation and correctness reasoning

Any path to u followed by edge (u,v) gives a valid candidate path to v. Taking its cost cannot worsen the current best bound. Repeated valid relaxations underpin shortest-path algorithms.

## Failure modes and assumptions

Dijkstra's greedy finalisation assumes nonnegative edge weights; a later negative edge can undermine the finalisation proof. A relaxation formula alone does not choose the correct algorithm.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: A path through u produces d[u]+weight; replace v's bound only if that candidate is smaller.**

Practise reciting the invariant or proof, not merely the equation.

**Interview problems:** Network Delay Time; Cheapest Flights Within K Stops.

**Research reference:** [Further mathematical detail](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/dijkstra.html). The examples and explanations here were independently developed.
